title: State Bank of India Returns to Dollar Bond Market With Planned $500 Million Issue
excerpt: India's largest lender is marketing five-year dollar bonds through its London branch, capitalizing on the RBI's new subsidized hedging facility that has made overseas borrowing cheaper than domestic funding.
body:
• SBI is marketing five-year dollar bonds through its London branch with initial price guidance of ~120 basis points over U.S. Treasuries
  • The bank expects to raise at least $500 million, with bankers saying the deal could reach $1 billion or more depending on demand
  • Fitch Ratings has assigned an expected BBB- rating to the proposed senior unsecured notes
  • The issue follows the RBI's June swap facility that slashes hedging costs, bringing the all-in landed cost to around 6.25%-6.50% — cheaper than domestic borrowing

SBI's Return to Public Dollar Debt

State Bank of India, the country's largest lender, is returning to the public dollar bond market after nearly a year, with plans to raise at least $500 million through five-year senior unsecured notes, three merchant bankers told Reuters this week.

The bonds will be issued through SBI's London branch, with initial price guidance set at roughly 120 basis points over U.S. Treasuries. The bank has begun marketing the bonds and expects to complete the sale by the end of the week, the bankers said, declining to be identified as they were not authorized to speak to the media.

Final pricing could tighten by as much as 30 basis points from the initial guidance, one banker said, adding that the deal size could reach $1 billion or more on strong investor demand. Fitch Ratings has assigned an expected BBB- rating to the proposed notes.

RBI's Swap Facility Changes the Math

The issue comes amid a rush by Indian banks to tap dollar bond markets after the Reserve Bank of India in June opened a swap facility that sharply reduces hedging costs for overseas borrowings by state-run companies.

Under the RBI's framework, external commercial borrowings with an average maturity of at least three years qualify for the swap facility at a fixed rate of 1.5% per annum, compounded semi-annually. The discount brings the all-in landed cost for lenders like SBI to around 6.25%-6.50%, which is cheaper than their local cost of borrowing, according to merchant bankers cited by Reuters.

"With 150 basis points of hedging discount, the all-in landed cost for these lenders should be around 6.25%-6.50%, which is cheaper than their local cost of borrowing."

— Merchant banker familiar with the deal

Merchant bankers expect inflows of $15 billion to $20 billion through this route over the next six months, signaling a broader shift in how Indian banks and state-owned companies fund themselves.

Building on a Year of Overseas Fundraising

SBI had planned to raise $1 billion through a public dollar bond issue in June but deferred the sale due to higher borrowing costs following heavy issuance by Indian lenders, according to Reuters. The bank subsequently raised $600 million through a private placement of three-year dollar bonds at a spread of 100 basis points over the Secured Overnight Financing Rate.

In early July, SBI raised another $300 million through three-year senior unsecured floating-rate notes at SOFR plus 100 basis points — one of the first large state-owned lenders to use the RBI's new facility, Mint reported.

SBI last tapped the public dollar bond market in September 2025, raising $500 million through five-year bonds at a coupon of 4.5%, a spread of 75 basis points over U.S. Treasuries — the tightest spread achieved by an Indian issuer at the time. That issuance drew orders exceeding $1.1 billion from 85 accounts.

A Crowded but Growing Market

Large private-sector lenders including HDFC Bank, Axis Bank, and ICICI Bank have already tapped dollar bond markets in June and July. Power Finance Corporation has also raised funds through the RBI's overseas borrowing window, according to Mint.

SBI's board approved raising up to $2 billion through overseas bond issuances in FY27, part of a broader plan to raise up to ₹60,000 crore through debt instruments including Basel III-compliant Additional Tier-I and Tier-II bonds, to support business growth and strengthen its capital base. As of March-end, the bank's capital-to-risk weighted assets ratio stood at 15.40%, with a common equity Tier-I ratio of 12.29%.

The dollar bond push follows S&P's upgrade of India's sovereign and SBI's rating from BBB- to BBB, which has improved pricing conditions for Indian issuers in global markets. Market participants expect more public-sector banks and state-owned companies to follow SBI's lead as the economics of foreign-currency borrowings improve under the RBI's framework.
nri_angle: India's largest bank raising capital internationally signals growing global confidence in Indian financial institutions, relevant to NRI investors tracking Indian banking stocks and bond markets.
